blocks.en: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" — Psalm 22:1 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Dios mío, Dios mío, ¿por qué me has desamparado?" — Salmo 22:1 (RVG)

blocks.en: 1. The Psalm of the Cross
blocks.es_reference: 1. El Salmo de la Cruz

blocks.en: Psalm 22 has been called "the Psalm of the Cross," and with good reason. Written by David roughly a thousand years before Jesus was born, it describes a scene of suffering so detailed and so specific that it reads less like the experience of an ancient king and more like an eyewitness account of Calvary. It opens with the very words our Lord cried from the cross, and it moves through pierced hands and feet, parched thirst, mocking onlookers, and gambling for the sufferer's clothing — and then, remarkably, it turns from agony to triumph and ends on a note of worldwide worship. This is one of the great Messianic psalms, a window opened a thousand years in advance onto the death and victory of Christ.
blocks.es_reference: El Salmo 22 ha sido llamado "el Salmo de la Cruz," y con buena razón. Escrito por David unos mil años antes de que naciera Jesús, describe una escena de sufrimiento tan detallada y tan específica que se lee menos como la experiencia de un antiguo rey y más como el relato de un testigo ocular del Calvario. Comienza con las mismas palabras que nuestro Señor clamó desde la cruz, y avanza por manos y pies traspasados, sed ardiente, espectadores burlones, y el sorteo de la ropa del que sufre — y entonces, asombrosamente, pasa de la agonía al triunfo y termina en una nota de adoración mundial. Este es uno de los grandes salmos mesiánicos, una ventana abierta mil años por adelantado a la muerte y la victoria de Cristo.

blocks.en: The Jewish people sang this psalm for centuries without fully understanding it. How could a song of such intimate suffering belong to David, who died in his bed an old man? The answer is that David, moved by the Spirit of God, was writing of someone greater than himself — the Son who would one day hang upon a Roman cross and carry the sins of the world.
blocks.es_reference: El pueblo judío cantó este salmo por siglos sin comprenderlo del todo. ¿Cómo podía un canto de sufrimiento tan íntimo pertenecer a David, que murió anciano en su cama? La respuesta es que David, movido por el Espíritu de Dios, escribía de alguien más grande que él mismo — el Hijo que un día colgaría de una cruz romana y cargaría los pecados del mundo.

blocks.en: 2. Philip and the Ethiopian
blocks.es_reference: 2. Felipe y el Etíope

blocks.en: Acts 8:35 (NKJV): "Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning at this Scripture, preached Jesus to him."
blocks.es_reference: Hechos 8:35 (RVG): "Entonces Felipe, abriendo su boca, y comenzando desde esta escritura, le predicó a Jesús."

blocks.en: In the book of Acts, an Ethiopian official is riding home in his chariot, reading aloud from the prophet Isaiah, when Philip is sent by the Spirit to join him. The man is puzzled: of whom does the prophet speak? Beginning at that very passage of Old Testament Scripture, Philip preached Jesus to him. Notice the lesson: the eunuch had only the Old Testament in his hands, yet that was enough, because the Old Testament is full of Christ. Philip took an ancient Hebrew text and from it preached the gospel. The same is true of Psalm 22. A person who has only the Old Testament has, in this single psalm, a portrait of the crucified and risen Savior clear enough to lead them to faith.
blocks.es_reference: En el libro de los Hechos, un oficial etíope va camino a casa en su carro, leyendo en voz alta al profeta Isaías, cuando el Espíritu envía a Felipe a acompañarlo. El hombre está perplejo: ¿de quién habla el profeta? Comenzando desde aquel mismo pasaje de la Escritura del Antiguo Testamento, Felipe le predicó a Jesús. Note la lección: el eunuco tenía solo el Antiguo Testamento en sus manos, y sin embargo eso bastó, porque el Antiguo Testamento está lleno de Cristo. Felipe tomó un antiguo texto hebreo y de él predicó el evangelio. Lo mismo es cierto del Salmo 22. Una persona que tiene solo el Antiguo Testamento posee, en este solo salmo, un retrato del Salvador crucificado y resucitado lo bastante claro como para llevarla a la fe.

blocks.en: 3. What It Means to Be "Fulfilled"
blocks.es_reference: 3. Lo que Significa ser "Cumplido"

blocks.en: When we say a psalm like this is "fulfilled" in Christ, we should understand what the word can mean, for it works in more than one way. According to careful students of Scripture, a prophecy may be fulfilled in at least three senses. First, there is direct prediction: something is clearly foretold and then comes to pass, as when Isaiah predicted the destruction of Babylon long before it fell. Second, there is foreshadowing: an earlier thing is a picture or type of something greater, as the animal sacrifices of the Old Testament foreshadowed and were fulfilled in the one sacrifice of Christ. Third, there is parallel or double reference: language that describes one event but also, under the Spirit's hand, describes another. Psalm 22 carries this third quality powerfully — David spoke out of his own anguish, yet the words reach far beyond him to the cross.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando decimos que un salmo como este es "cumplido" en Cristo, conviene entender lo que la palabra puede significar, pues obra de más de una manera. Según los estudiosos cuidadosos de la Escritura, una profecía puede cumplirse en al menos tres sentidos. Primero, está la predicción directa: algo es claramente anunciado y luego sucede, como cuando Isaías predijo la destrucción de Babilonia mucho antes de que cayera. Segundo, está la prefiguración: una cosa anterior es figura o tipo de algo mayor, como los sacrificios de animales del Antiguo Testamento prefiguraban y fueron cumplidos en el único sacrificio de Cristo. Tercero, está la referencia paralela o doble: lenguaje que describe un evento pero también, bajo la mano del Espíritu, describe otro. El Salmo 22 lleva esta tercera cualidad poderosamente — David habló desde su propia angustia, pero las palabras alcanzan mucho más allá de él hasta la cruz.

blocks.en: 4. The Cry of Loneliness
blocks.es_reference: 4. El Clamor de Soledad

blocks.en: Psalm 22:1 (NKJV): "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me? Why are You so far from helping Me, and from the words of My groaning?"
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 22:1 (RVG): "Dios mío, Dios mío, ¿por qué me has desamparado? ¿Por qué estás tan lejos de mi salvación, y de las palabras de mi clamor?"

blocks.en: These are the first recorded words Jesus cried from the cross, quoting this psalm directly: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" Of all the pains of the crucifixion, this was the deepest. The Father had been with the Son throughout His entire life — at His baptism, on the mountain, in the garden. Why abandon Him now, in the darkest hour? The answer is the heart of the gospel: in that moment the Son was bearing the sin of the world, and a holy God turned His face away from the sin His Son carried. Jesus endured the forsakenness we deserved so that we might never be forsaken. He was cut off from God so that we could be brought near.
blocks.es_reference: Estas son las primeras palabras registradas que Jesús clamó desde la cruz, citando este salmo directamente: "Dios mío, Dios mío, ¿por qué me has desamparado?" De todos los dolores de la crucifixión, este fue el más profundo. El Padre había estado con el Hijo a lo largo de toda Su vida — en Su bautismo, en el monte, en el huerto. ¿Por qué abandonarlo ahora, en la hora más oscura? La respuesta es el corazón del evangelio: en ese momento el Hijo cargaba el pecado del mundo, y un Dios santo apartó Su rostro del pecado que Su Hijo llevaba. Jesús soportó el desamparo que nosotros merecíamos para que nosotros nunca fuéramos desamparados. Fue cortado de Dios para que nosotros pudiéramos ser acercados.

blocks.en: 5. The Suffering Described
blocks.es_reference: 5. El Sufrimiento Descrito

blocks.en: Psalm 22:14, 16 (NKJV): "I am poured out like water, and all My bones are out of joint … They pierced My hands and My feet."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 22:14, 16 (RVG): "Heme escurrido como aguas, y todos mis huesos se descoyuntaron … horadaron mis manos y mis pies."

blocks.en: The middle of the psalm reads like a medical description of death by crucifixion, written centuries before that form of execution was practiced. "I am poured out like water, and all My bones are out of joint" describes a body hanging by its own weight, joints pulled apart. "My heart is like wax; it has melted within Me" speaks of the failing heart. And then the most astonishing line of all: "They pierced My hands and My feet" — a precise picture of crucifixion set down by a man who had never seen one. David died of old age; his hands and feet were never pierced. He was describing Another. Around the cross the soldiers gambled for Jesus' garments, just as the psalm says, "They divide My garments among them, and for My clothing they cast lots" (Psalm 22:18).
blocks.es_reference: La parte central del salmo se lee como una descripción médica de la muerte por crucifixión, escrita siglos antes de que esa forma de ejecución se practicara. "Heme escurrido como aguas, y todos mis huesos se descoyuntaron" describe un cuerpo que cuelga por su propio peso, con las articulaciones separadas. "Mi corazón fue como cera, derritiéndose en medio de mis entrañas" habla del corazón que desfallece. Y luego la línea más asombrosa de todas: "horadaron mis manos y mis pies" — un cuadro preciso de la crucifixión puesto por escrito por un hombre que jamás había visto una. David murió de viejo; sus manos y sus pies nunca fueron traspasados. Describía a Otro. Alrededor de la cruz los soldados sortearon las vestiduras de Jesús, tal como dice el salmo: "Repartieron entre sí mis vestidos, y sobre mi ropa echaron suertes" (Salmo 22:18).

blocks.en: 6. From Agony to Triumph
blocks.es_reference: 6. De la Agonía al Triunfo

blocks.en: If the psalm ended at the suffering, it would be only a tragedy. But it does not end there. About halfway through, the tone turns. The sufferer who cried out in abandonment begins to declare the faithfulness of God, and by the close the psalm has become a great hymn of victory. It looks forward to a day when "all the ends of the world shall remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations shall worship before You" (Psalm 22:27).
blocks.es_reference: Si el salmo terminara en el sufrimiento, sería solo una tragedia. Pero no termina allí. Hacia la mitad, el tono cambia. El que sufría y clamaba en abandono comienza a declarar la fidelidad de Dios, y para el final el salmo se ha convertido en un gran himno de victoria. Mira adelante a un día cuando "se acordarán y se volverán a Jehová todos los confines de la tierra; y todas las familias de las naciones adorarán delante de ti" (Salmo 22:27).

blocks.en: Psalm 22:30-31 (NKJV): "A posterity shall serve Him. It will be recounted of the Lord to the next generation, they will come and declare His righteousness to a people who will be born, that He has done this."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 22:30-31 (RVG): "La posteridad le servirá; esto será contado de Jehová por generación. Vendrán, y anunciarán su justicia; a pueblo que ha de nacer, anunciarán que él hizo esto."

blocks.en: "That He has done this" — the Hebrew carries the sense of a finished work, and it is striking that one of the last words Jesus spoke from the cross was, "It is finished." The psalm that opened with the first cry of the cross closes with the last. From the deepest darkness, the work of salvation is accomplished, and the news of it goes out to a people not yet born — to us.
blocks.es_reference: "Que él hizo esto" — el hebreo lleva el sentido de una obra terminada, y es notable que una de las últimas palabras que Jesús habló desde la cruz fue: "Consumado es." El salmo que abrió con el primer clamor de la cruz cierra con el último. Desde la más profunda oscuridad, la obra de la salvación se cumple, y la noticia de ella sale a un pueblo aún no nacido — a nosotros.

blocks.en: 7. A Springboard for the Gospel
blocks.es_reference: 7. Un Trampolín para el Evangelio

blocks.en: Because Psalm 22 is so vivid a portrait of Christ drawn entirely from the Hebrew Scriptures, it is one of the most useful passages in the Bible for sharing the gospel with someone who honors the Old Testament but does not yet know Jesus. Like Philip with the Ethiopian, a believer can begin right at this Scripture and preach Jesus. Imagine sitting with a Jewish friend who has only the Old Testament in his home. You need not argue; you need only open Psalm 22 together and read it slowly. Who is this sufferer, forsaken, with garments gambled away, whose anguish ends in worldwide worship? The text raises the question; the Spirit answers it. (One honest note of preparation: some Hebrew manuscripts of verse 16 read "like a lion" rather than "pierced" — a difference of a single Hebrew letter. Older manuscript evidence, including the Dead Sea Scrolls, favors "pierced," which is why nearly every translation reads that way — but a well-read Jewish friend may raise the question, and it is better to know the issue than to be caught off guard by it.)
blocks.es_reference: Porque el Salmo 22 es un retrato tan vívido de Cristo trazado enteramente de las Escrituras hebreas, es uno de los pasajes más útiles de la Biblia para compartir el evangelio con alguien que honra el Antiguo Testamento pero aún no conoce a Jesús. Como Felipe con el etíope, un creyente puede comenzar justo desde esta Escritura y predicar a Jesús. Imagine sentarse con un amigo judío que tiene solo el Antiguo Testamento en su casa. No necesita discutir; solo necesita abrir juntos el Salmo 22 y leerlo despacio. ¿Quién es este que sufre, desamparado, cuyas vestiduras son sorteadas, y cuya angustia termina en adoración mundial? El texto plantea la pregunta; el Espíritu la responde. (Una nota honesta de preparación: algunos manuscritos hebreos del versículo 16 leen «como león» en vez de «traspasaron» — una diferencia de una sola letra hebrea. La evidencia manuscrita más antigua, incluyendo los Rollos del Mar Muerto, favorece «traspasaron», por lo cual casi todas las traducciones dicen eso — pero un amigo judío bien informado puede plantear la pregunta, y es mejor conocer el asunto que ser tomado por sorpresa.)

blocks.en: Two Friends, One Psalm: A helpful way to learn this is to practice it with a partner. One person takes the role of a Christian, the other the role of a Jewish friend who has only the Old Testament. Using Psalm 22 as the starting point — and drawing in other Scriptures from memory as needed — the believer walks gently through the psalm and presents the plan of salvation, showing how this thousand-year-old song points unmistakably to Jesus. Then the partners switch roles. Working through it aloud fixes the truth in the heart and builds the confidence to do it for real when God opens the door.
blocks.es_reference: Dos Amigos, un Salmo: Una manera útil de aprender esto es practicarlo con un compañero. Una persona toma el papel de un cristiano, la otra el papel de un amigo judío que tiene solo el Antiguo Testamento. Usando el Salmo 22 como punto de partida — e incorporando otras Escrituras de memoria según haga falta — el creyente recorre con suavidad el salmo y presenta el plan de salvación, mostrando cómo este canto de mil años de antigüedad señala inequívocamente a Jesús. Luego los compañeros intercambian papeles. Trabajarlo en voz alta fija la verdad en el corazón y edifica la confianza para hacerlo de veras cuando Dios abra la puerta.

blocks.en: 8. The God Who Was Forsaken for Us
blocks.es_reference: 8. El Dios que Fue Desamparado por Nosotros

blocks.en: Psalm 22 is finally not about David's suffering or even chiefly about the mechanics of crucifixion. It is about love. It shows us a Savior who went into the darkness on purpose, who heard no answer to His cry so that we would never be met with silence, who was poured out like water so that we could be filled. The same psalm that records the lowest point of human history records its greatest turning point, for the death it describes became the doorway to life for all the families of the earth.
blocks.es_reference: El Salmo 22 no trata al final del sufrimiento de David ni principalmente de los mecanismos de la crucifixión. Trata del amor. Nos muestra un Salvador que entró en la oscuridad a propósito, que no oyó respuesta a Su clamor para que nosotros nunca fuéramos recibidos con silencio, que fue derramado como agua para que nosotros pudiéramos ser llenados. El mismo salmo que registra el punto más bajo de la historia humana registra su mayor punto de cambio, pues la muerte que describe se convirtió en la puerta a la vida para todas las familias de la tierra.

blocks.en: When you read this psalm, do not read it as a distant prophecy only. Read it as a personal gift. The forsaken One was forsaken for you. The pierced hands were pierced for you. And the finished work is finished for you. The proper response to Psalm 22 is the response the psalm itself calls for at its end: to remember, to turn to the LORD, and to worship Him among the great congregation of those who have been redeemed.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando lea este salmo, no lo lea solo como una profecía distante. Léalo como un regalo personal. El que fue desamparado fue desamparado por usted. Las manos traspasadas fueron traspasadas por usted. Y la obra terminada está terminada por usted. La respuesta apropiada al Salmo 22 es la respuesta que el salmo mismo pide al final: acordarse, volverse a Jehová, y adorarle entre la gran congregación de los que han sido redimidos.

sa.prompt: Explain why Psalm 22 is called "the Psalm of the Cross," and why it cannot be only about David himself.
sa.model: Psalm 22 is called "the Psalm of the Cross" because it describes crucifixion in vivid detail about a thousand years before Jesus was born, and centuries before crucifixion was even practiced. It opens with the very cry Jesus uttered from the cross and goes on to picture pierced hands and feet, mocking onlookers, and the dividing of garments. It cannot be only about David himself, because David died an old man in his bed; his hands and feet were never pierced, and he never suffered what the psalm describes. Moved by the Spirit of God, David was writing of Someone greater than himself, the coming Messiah.

sa.prompt: What does the account of Philip and the Ethiopian (Acts 8) teach about preaching Christ from the Old Testament?
sa.model: In Acts 8 Philip met an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah but not understanding it. Beginning at that very passage of Scripture, Philip preached Jesus to him, and the man believed and was baptized. The account teaches that the Old Testament is full of Christ and that we can preach Him straight from its pages. The Ethiopian had only the Hebrew Scriptures, yet they were enough to lead him to faith once someone showed him the Christ they pointed to. Like Philip, we can begin where a person already is in the Scriptures and from there preach Jesus.

sa.prompt: Describe the three senses in which a prophecy can be "fulfilled," with an example of each.
sa.model: The lesson describes three senses in which a prophecy can be "fulfilled." One is direct prediction, where a prophet foretells a specific event before it happens, as Isaiah foretold the fall of Babylon. Another is the fulfilling of a type or pattern, where an earlier person or event foreshadows a later one. The third, which Psalm 22 carries so powerfully, is parallel or double reference: words that describe one situation in the writer's own life and also, beyond it, point to a greater fulfillment. Psalm 22 speaks of David's anguish, but its deeper reference is to the suffering of Christ on the cross.

sa.prompt: Explain the cry of Psalm 22:1 and why it was the deepest pain of the crucifixion.
sa.model: Psalm 22:1 opens, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?", the very words Jesus cried from the cross. The lesson says this was the deepest pain of the crucifixion, deeper than the nails or the mockery. The physical agony was terrible, but the worst was the forsakenness, the moment the Son bore the sin of the world and a holy God turned His face away from that sin. Jesus had never been separated from the Father, and now He felt that separation in our place. The cry reveals that the cross was not merely a physical death but a spiritual abandonment endured for us.

sa.prompt: According to the lesson, what did Jesus accomplish for us by enduring the forsakenness of the cross?
sa.model: By enduring the forsakenness of the cross, Jesus accomplished our salvation: He took the separation from God that our sin deserved, so that we who believe might never be forsaken. The Son was abandoned for a time so that we would never be abandoned for eternity. He bore the cry "why have You forsaken Me?" so that we could be welcomed in. This is the heart of the gospel in Psalm 22: the Savior went into the darkness on purpose, in our place, taking what was ours so that He could give us what was His, unbroken fellowship with God.

sa.prompt: Describe how the middle of Psalm 22 reads like a description of crucifixion, citing specific details.
sa.model: The middle of Psalm 22 reads like an eyewitness description of crucifixion written centuries before it existed. It speaks of bones out of joint, a heart melted like wax, strength dried up, and a tongue cleaving to the jaws, all marks of that slow death. Most strikingly it says, "They pierced My hands and My feet," the precise method of crucifixion. It describes enemies staring and gloating, and the dividing of garments and casting lots for clothing, exactly as the soldiers did at Calvary. The detail is so exact that the psalm can only be a Spirit-given portrait of the cross.

sa.prompt: Explain how Psalm 22 turns from agony to triumph, and how its ending connects to Jesus' words "It is finished."
sa.model: About halfway through, Psalm 22 turns from agony to triumph. The sufferer who cried out in abandonment begins to praise God and to declare His name to the congregation, and the psalm ends with worship reaching to the ends of the earth and to a people yet to be born. The closing phrase, "that He has done this," connects to one of Jesus' last words from the cross, "It is finished." The work was accomplished. So the psalm moves from the darkness of the cross to the victory of the finished work, from the cry of dereliction to worldwide worship of the risen Lord.

sa.prompt: Explain why Psalm 22 is so useful for sharing the gospel, and how a believer might use it like Philip did.
sa.model: Psalm 22 is especially useful for sharing the gospel because it is a vivid portrait of Christ drawn entirely from the Hebrew Scriptures. For anyone who honors the Old Testament, it shows the suffering and triumph of the Messiah from a source they already respect. A believer might use it as Philip used Isaiah: opening the psalm with a friend, walking through its astonishing detail of the cross, and from there pointing to Jesus as the One it describes. It lets us begin with Scripture the other person trusts and lead them gently to the Christ those words foretold.

sa.prompt: The lesson suggests a practice exercise for learning to witness from Psalm 22. Explain how the exercise works and why it is valuable.
sa.model: The lesson suggests a practice exercise done with a partner. One person plays a Christian and the other plays a Jewish friend who honors the Old Testament; the Christian presents Christ from Psalm 22, showing how its details point to Jesus. Then the partners switch roles, so each gets practice making the case. The exercise is valuable because witnessing is a skill that grows with practice, not just knowledge. Working through Psalm 22 aloud with another believer builds confidence and familiarity, so that when a real conversation comes, we are ready to open the Scriptures and point someone to Christ.

sa.prompt: According to the close of the lesson, what is Psalm 22 finally about, and how should we read it personally?
sa.model: According to the close of the lesson, Psalm 22 is finally about love, a Savior who went into the darkness on purpose for us. It is not merely a remarkable prophecy to admire from a distance; it is meant to be read personally. The psalm itself ends by calling for a threefold response: remember what God has done, turn to the LORD, and worship Him. So we read Psalm 22 not as spectators but as those for whom Christ was forsaken, letting its picture of the cross move us to remember His love, return to Him, and bow in worship before the One who did this for us.
